title: 2 No-Brainer Warren Buffett Stocks to Buy in the Post-Election Market Sell-Off and Hold Forever

Is it best to stay away from equity markets right now, given the significant uncertainty created by the recent U.S. midterm elections? Some might think so. After all, stocks fell significantly following the elections. However, it's important for investors not to focus too much on short-term volatility. That's a core investing principle that Warren Buffett, arguably the greatest investor of all time, has stressed time and time again.

In times like this, it's important to stay the course and look for stocks to buy that are worth holding onto forever. Let's consider two stocks Warren Buffett loves that fit the bill: Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) and Coca-Cola (NYSE:KO).

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.

1. Alphabet

While Warren Buffett has historically avoided tech stocks, he made an exception last year when he engineered Berkshire Hathaway's (NYSE:BRKA) (NYSE:BRKB) investment in Alphabet. Since that initial investment, the conglomerate has bought additional shares. Clearly, Buffett and other leaders at Berkshire Hathaway are bullish on Alphabet's prospects, and with good reason. The tech leader has many qualities that Buffett loves.

One of the most important is its wide moat -- something every company that performs well over long periods tends to have. Alphabet's moat stems from its data flywheel. The company's leading search engine, Google, enables it to collect massive amounts of data on search preferences, which helps it improve results and boost search volume.

Alphabet's advertising business still generates most of its revenue, but the company's cloud computing segment, Google Cloud, has been growing much faster in recent quarters. In the third quarter, Alphabet's total revenue increased by 25% year over year to $127.6 billion.

Cloud revenue jumped 103% year over year to $30.7 billion. The company's earnings per share dropped 26% year over year to $2.12, while its free cash flow was a negative $9.1 billion, versus a positive $24.5 billion in the year-ago period. Alphabet is doubling down on its artificial intelligence (AI)-related investments, which partly explains the significant decline in free cash flow.

Some investors are worried that these investments might not pay off. But considering Alphabet's strength in the cloud industry -- particularly in offering AI-related services -- my view is that the tech giant's investments are justified. Further, the cloud industry remains underpenetrated, providing the company with a massive long-term tailwind.

title: A little-known 31-year-old trader shorted Nvidia — it’s down around 27% since. Is his bet paying off?
detail:
A little-known 31-year-old trader shorted Nvidia — it’s down around 27% since. Is his bet paying off?
Chris Morris
Thu, November 12, 2026 at 2:45 PM MST 4 min read
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

As investors digest the resignation of Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) CEO and president Jensen Huang following two alleged affairs, including one with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, it's inevitable that some traders are going to brag they saw the problem coming. That may or may not be true. None, however, saw it as early as Christian Lamarco.

Lamarco's Culper Research isn't the best known short-selling and investment research firm, but it was the only company to flag "a significant China problem" at Nvidia as far back as May.

Culper, in that note, said it was shorting Nvidia — and that could be one of the best calls on Wall Street this year. Since the firm researched the note, Nvidia shares have fallen more than 27% (as of 11:00 a.m. ET on Thursday). That would represent a profit of more than $60 per shorted share.

An 'uncomfortably close relationship'

The 40-page report raised concerns about the size of Nvidia's business in China and flagged an "uncomfortably close relationship" between then-CEO Jensen Huang and Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. (Huang is a common surname and the two are not related.)

Lemarco said he was mocked after issuing the report. Even that was more attention the three-person firm would usually receive.

Now, however, people are more likely to listen.

"Sometimes, people care about what you have to say. Sometimes, they don't," Lamarco told The Wall Street Journal. "I guess in this case, they cared six months later."

Read More: Vanguard reveals what's coming for U.S. stocks — and it could be bad news for this group of investors

Profits for prescience?

What's unclear is just how much, if anything, Lamarco and Culper Research made off of the decision to short Nvidia. While the chipmaker has lost over $1 trillion in market value since the report was issued, Lamarco has declined to say how much his call has earned the firm. He also has not said whether he is still shorting the stock.

Nvidia wasn't the first company Culper has targeted. Since it was founded in 2019, it has turned its sights on several public companies, generally small-cap ones. It's not afraid to make noise, though. One founder, for instance, hired Elon Musk's attorney to sue for defamation after Culper alleged his company was tied to the Sinaloa drug cartel. The most recent target is Cerebras Systems, an AI hardware and supercomputer company, which labels the company "hot garbage."
